data.title: Aseanâs fashion trade faces new survival rules
data.description:
FOR decades, Asean fashion grew by mastering a simple rule of survival: produce fast, scale volume, and win on price. This playbook built a regional fashion and textile industry on track to cross US$50 billion in market value.

Today, that has entirely changed. Mandatory disclosures on supply chain emissions are coming into effect across major import markets like the United States in 2027, while brands within the European Union will face stricter supply chain due diligence obligations starting 2028.

Suppliers and manufacturers who don’t meet – or simply don’t have the data to prove that they meet these standards will soon be locked out of global trade.

For Asean, which has emerged as the dominant manufacturing bloc for the US and EU, the new rule for survival is sustainability literacy.

The readiness gap

As it stands, while Asean is scaling in production, it is falling behind on accountability. Recent findings from the Singapore Fashion Council (SFC) highlight a significant opportunity to strengthen preparedness for these new reporting requirements.

For example, only 43 per cent of regional manufacturers currently track their greenhouse gas emissions.

Water consumption also appears to be a blind spot, where none of the manufacturers surveyed report that they measure their water consumption or have plans to begin tracking it.

In fact, fashion is merely the canary in the coal mine. From electronics to agri-food and automotive, heightened scrutiny on ESG makes one thing clear: no export-reliant industry in Asean will remain insulated from transparency requirements.

To survive and indeed, thrive, under these new rules, Asean companies must treat sustainability literacy as a commercial capability that needs to be actively built.

New rules for survival

The first rule is about starting with clarity, not perfection.

Businesses must familiarise themselves with emissions accounting guidance from regulatory requirements and recognised standards in the textile and apparel sector. This will help them to prioritise focus areas and select short-term goals that can already demonstrate success.

Many mistakenly believe that they need complex, costly carbon-accounting software right on day one. But they can start with simple baselines, like tracking office energy use or basic factory waste, and build internal capability before attempting to tackle more complex areas like the supply chain emissions of downstream partners.

Leveraging localised platforms like the Singapore Emission Factors Registry database or the new Sustainability Readiness Intelligence tool can also take much of the initial complexity and friction out of emissions reporting.

The next rule for survival demands collaboration.

Fashion and textile supply chains are tightly interconnected, where design decisions can contribute up to 80 per cent of a product’s environmental impact.

Co-creating with suppliers from the earliest stages of production allows brands to design out waste, extend product lifespans and keep materials in circulation longer.

A good example is zipper manufacturer YKK, which has developed its Revive series using zippers made from recycled plastic bottles. The design allows consumers to replace a broken slider easily from the top stop, rather than discarding an otherwise perfectly good jacket.

It is a practical illustration of how collaboration and thoughtful design can support circularity while helping consumers extend the lifespan of their clothing.

Customers are also key downstream partners in these efforts. Whether through take-back schemes or partnering local tailors for affordable mending services, brands and retailers can empower customers to keep their garments in use for longer.

Making circularity convenient is what turns consumers into active allies for waste reduction.

Finally, the third rule mandates that businesses communicate with credibility. Broad marketing claims such as “eco-friendly”, “green” or “conscious” are increasingly subject to scrutiny from both regulators and consumers.

The SFC’s data also highlights how credible, substantiated sustainability claims can be a key differentiator for Singapore enterprises seeking to build partnerships and enter new markets, both domestically and across Asean.

In today’s increasingly discerning marketplace, transparency and evidence-based claims, such as disclosing exact recycled material ratios and meeting recognised certification standards, are essential to building trust and unlocking business opportunities.

Honesty is fundamental. Partners and consumers respect realistic progress over impossible perfection. Demonstrating quick, achievable wins while acknowledging gaps builds market credibility that goes a long way.

Claiming Asean’s seat at the table

Ultimately, no brand, manufacturer or supplier can own this new playbook alone.

The scale of Scope 3 emissions and supply chain fragmentation across Asean demands a unified, ecosystem approach. The clock is ticking.

By moving from transactional vendor relationships to genuine co-creation, and from vague marketing claims to audited data transparency and traceability, the region’s fashion industry can turn a compliance threat into a lasting trade advantage.

The choice ahead is clear: rather than wait for global markets to dictate the future, we can claim our seat at the table and shape the evolution of sustainable fashion.

The writer is chief executive officer at the Singapore Fashion Council

data.title: China factory activity eases into decline as growth wobbles
data.description:
[BEIJING] China’s factory activity slowed in October, underscoring the challenges facing policymakers as they seek to sustain an economic recovery to ensure this year’s growth target is met.

The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) fell to 49.3 from 50.1 in September, the National Bureau of Statistics said Saturday (Oct 31). That compares with the median forecast of 49.9 in a Bloomberg survey of economists. A reading above 50 indicates expansion.

The non-manufacturing measure of activity in construction and services came in at 49.7, versus 50.2 in September.

The deterioration suggests the world’s second-largest economy has lost some traction at the start of the fourth quarter, following a modest rebound in the prior three months.

Beijing may face more pressure to provide additional support after introducing a fresh package of targeted stimulus measures in recent weeks, as policymakers seek to keep growth on track to meet the government’s annual target of 4.5 to 5 per cent.

The weakness extended across both supply and demand, with the manufacturing production index falling 1.9 percentage points to 49.8 and the new-orders gauge dropping 1.1 percentage points to 49.4, according to the statistics bureau. Large manufacturers remained in expansion at 50.2, while the measures for medium-sized and small firms fell to 48.4 and 47.5 respectively.

The high-tech manufacturing PMI was 51.3, expanding even as overall factory activity contracted.

The government has already dialed up policies to bolster the economy, offering more credit support for small businesses and consumers, mortgage subsidies for some homebuyers and additional bond quotas for local governments. 

Construction on major infrastructure projects such as Six Networks has also been rolled out, and the authorities have signalled a willingness to introduce further measures if necessary. BLOOMBERG

data.title: OpenAI slashes funding target by US$10 billion amid tech rout: FT
data.description:
[BENGALURU] OpenAI has slashed the target for its latest funding round by US$10 billion amid a sell-off in tech stocks driven by artificial intelligence worries, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about US$20 billion and its desired valuation has dropped to US$1.25 trillion from US$1.4 billion, the report said.

OpenAI set a Friday (Oct 30) deadline for investors to commit to the funding round, but the “first close” is expected to raise less than US$20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, it added.

A consortium of United Arab Emirates investors that includes state-backed technology fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant in the round, and as part of the deal, OpenAI would gain the option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region, the newspaper added.

Venture capital firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to the report.

Wealthy individuals will have the option to invest in a subsequent retail offering at a US$1.25 trillion valuation, FT added.

OpenAI, MGX, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours. Founders Fund could not be reached for comment.

US tech stocks have suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive spending on AI. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 2.9 per cent on Friday and is down 7.8 per cent from its all-time closing high reached on Oct 6.

OpenAI, which is pursuing a listing in 2027, has been keen to close the funding round partly to get ahead of Anthropic’s imminent listing as the two are tapping a similar investor base, Reuters reported. REUTERS

data.title: Half of Americansâ spending goes to housing and food, most in 15 years
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Housing and food made up nearly half of US households’ spending in 2025, the most in 15 years amid rising rents, homeowner costs and beef prices.

On average, American families spent US$1,988 more on the two categories combined than in 2024, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. And that was before the Iran war sent some grocery prices and utility costs surging this year.

At the same time, average pretax income rose 6.4 per cent to US$110,847 in 2025, outpacing both inflation and expenditures, the annual Consumer Expenditure Survey showed. 

The figures helped explain the tension between improving household finances and downbeat views of the economy, and why affordability is a central issue in the upcoming midterm elections. While Americans had more money coming in, more of what they spent went to necessities.

Food and housing – which includes rent, utilities and household furniture – were the only two major spending categories to post statistically significant increases last year, according to the BLS. 

Housing remained the largest household expense, accounting for 33.9 per cent of total expenditures. Excluding a jump in 2020 after Covid hit, that share was the highest since 2010.

The share of spending Americans dedicate to food, meanwhile, has been rising since 2020 and at 13 per cent is now the highest since 2011. The dollar value of the food budget – up 4.6 per cent to US$10,633 in 2025 – outpaced the increase in total spending.

Americans spent US$1,579 on meat, poultry, fish and eggs last year. That’s 11.7 per cent more than in 2024 and twice as much as in 2010.

Those products accounted for about 24 per cent of grocery spending in 2025, up from 19 per cent in 2023. Over those two years, protein accounted for about 95 per cent of the increase in average food-at-home spending. BLOOMBERG

data.title: The AI frenzy gets a reality check
data.description:
THE initial euphoria over artificial intelligence has hit a speed bump. For the past three years, the market has treated every dollar spent on AI as a downpayment on the future. But over the past month, it has started asking some hard questions.

Shares in the hyperscalers – Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta – have fallen, and the selling has spread to the chipmakers and cloud providers that supply them.

The S&P 500, which is heavily weighted towards the hyperscalers and chipmaker Nvidia, is barely above its August peak. In the month to Oct 23, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was down 14 per cent. The biggest listed specialist AI cloud provider, CoreWeave, has lost more than 38 per cent.

Meanwhile, Treasury bonds, the classic safe haven for investors, have rallied despite rising inflation, which normally leads them to fall.

No single piece of bad news explains this performance. Rather, investors appear to be confronting a question that the euphoria had made them defer: Can the revenue from AI ever catch up with the spending?

The sums involved are staggering. The four big hyperscalers alone are on course to spend roughly US$700 billion on capital expenditure in 2026 and close to US$1 trillion in 2027, most of it on data centres and the chips that fill them.

Lessons from past manias

In sheer scale, the AI build-out invites comparison with the great infrastructure booms of the past: the railway manias of Victorian Britain and Gilded Age America, and the fibre-optic and dot-com frenzies of the late 1990s.

Those precedents were premised on the notion that transformative technologies justify heavy spending. They are better read as a warning. Each was a vast bet on future demand, and each ended in a bust.

Britain’s railway mania collapsed in 1847, wiping out thousands of investors. In America, overbuilt lines helped trigger the panics of the late 19th century. Telecommunications carriers poured roughly US$500 billion into networks in the late 1990s, and by 2002 the Nasdaq had lost almost 80 per cent of its value.

In every case, the infrastructure went on to transform the economy, but the early investors who paid for it mostly did not share in the gains.

Each boom overestimated how quickly demand would grow. The problem was not the technology but the timing.

By 2001, only a small, single-digit fraction of the fibre laid in America was actually operational. The network eventually filled up – it carries today’s internet traffic – but not before one-time telecom giants WorldCom, Global Crossing and dozens of others had collapsed.

The same mismatch is visible now. Data centre construction is following an exponential curve, with each year’s plans dwarfing the last.

But AI adoption is not exponential. It seems to advance in fits and starts: first, there is a burst of enthusiasm; then, a long plateau as organisations work out how to reorganise around deploying a new tool; and then, maybe another leap.

A widely cited Massachusetts Institute of Technology study in July 2025 found that 95 per cent of organisations saw no measurable positive return on investment after six months. It is organisations, not individuals, that will drive most AI revenue.

The revenue gap

No hyperscaler is likely to be making money on generative AI. Microsoft and Amazon, the only two to disclose AI revenue, report a combined annualised revenue of US$60 billion to US$70 billion – against around US$400 billion in capital spending between them in 2026 alone.

By some estimates, covering current and planned AI capex through identifiable AI income would require something like US$2.5 trillion a year – more than the combined revenue of the entire technology sector today.

Meanwhile, valuations across much of the AI ecosystem have run far ahead of earnings. Today’s share prices make sense only if AI delivers productivity gains far larger than anything yet visible in the data. That doesn’t mean the bet is wrong.

But investors are paying now for a transformation that may arrive much later, and patience is finite. Markets need not conclude that AI is a failure to reprice it sharply. They need only decide that the payoff is further off than they had assumed.

Money that goes in circles

What further complicates the story is the way the industry finances itself. A growing share of AI demand rests on recycled capital, vendor financing and promises of future purchases.

For example, Nvidia has invested US$30 billion in OpenAI, which will in turn fill its data centres with Nvidia chips and has guaranteed up to US$105 billion in leases on a data centre campus that will host its chips for OpenAI. Nvidia holds a stake in CoreWeave, a cloud provider that buys its chips, and has agreed to purchase capacity that CoreWeave cannot sell.

Oracle has booked a contract worth around US$300 billion to supply computing power to OpenAI, a company still losing billions of dollars a year.

In such arrangements, one company’s capital expenditure becomes another’s revenue. Reported growth can stay spectacular without proving that the ecosystem has a self-sustaining economic model. When suppliers fund customers who then buy from those same suppliers, separating genuine demand from financial engineering becomes difficult.

The question is not whether demand exists – it does. The question is whether it will eventually generate enough revenue from customers outside the AI ecosystem – the banks, retailers, hospitals and manufacturers that must ultimately pay the bills – to justify the capital already committed.

Borrowing against the future

Debt adds another layer of risk. Since 2025, bond issuance has funded a rising share of AI capital spending, as even the cash-rich hyperscalers have turned to credit markets to raise money.

Hyperscaler bond issuance soared from around US$17 billion in 2024 to US$109 billion in 2025 and US$194 billion in the first half of 2026.

Meta raised US$30 billion in a single bond sale and arranged a further US$27 billion for its Hyperion data centre in Louisiana through an off-balance-sheet vehicle with private credit provider Blue Owl Capital. Oracle, more stretched than its peers, has borrowed heavily to meet its OpenAI commitments.

Credit markets have noticed. Trading in credit default swaps (CDS) on hyperscalers and their suppliers, which insure against defaults, has surged, with Oracle’s spreads serving as the bellwether of what traders now call the AI hyperscaler default trade.

The volumes of CDS linked to seven AI-linked companies traded more than US$9 billion a week in September, up more than fourfold from the US$2 billion weekly average in July.

What worries these investors is not an outright collapse. The problem is that debt has been raised against forecasts that assume AI spending will keep accelerating, while interest and lease payments are fixed. The real test of resilience, then, is not whether the cycle can survive a collapse in spending, but whether it can survive spending that merely stops accelerating.

Chips with a short shelf life

There is reason to think this cycle could be harsher on investors than its predecessors. Railway track and fibre-optic cable stayed productive for decades; later investors who bought bankrupt networks for cents on the dollar did very well out of them.

Graphics processing units (GPUs) – the chips that power AI – offer no such consolation. New chips outperform older ones so quickly that a GPU may pay its way for only two to five years. And if data centre construction is delayed, the chips that firms buy may have to remain in storage and run the risk of becoming obsolete.

Data Center Watch counts roughly US$200 billion worth of projects blocked or delayed by local opposition in the first half of 2026 alone.

Projects have also been held back by power and building shortages. Microsoft’s CEO, Satya Nadella, warned as early as November 2025 that the company might end up with “a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in”.

None of this means AI is a mirage. It will almost certainly transform economies, productivity and work over the coming decades, as the railways and the internet did before it. But current valuations and investment levels assume that transformation will happen faster, and more profitably, than the evidence supports.

The web of cross-shareholdings and circular financing leaves the industry exposed to any loss of confidence, anywhere in the chain. When reality falls short of inflated expectations, as it usually does, a painful correction looks likely. The past month may prove to be only the first instalment. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Apple overtakes Nvidia to become worldâs most valuable company
data.description:
[SAN FRANCISCO] Apple reclaimed the title of world’s most valuable company on Friday (Oct 30), taking the mantle from Nvidia as investors seek the perceived safety of the iPhone maker amid concerns about artificial intelligence spending.

Shares of Apple fell 1.2 per cent on Friday, resulting in a market capitalisation of US$5.03 trillion, while Nvidia sank 4.2 per cent to close with a valuation of US$4.93 trillion. This is the first time Apple has overtaken Nvidia since briefly doing so in late July.

Friday’s sell-off came as a number of major technology companies disappointed with their results, including Intel and Amazon.com, which followed similarly disappointing reports from Alphabet and Meta Platforms, among others. The reports renewed concerns about the outlook for AI spending, something Apple has largely foregone. 

Fears that heavy spending on AI computing infrastructure won’t pay off have helped make Apple, which has kept a lid on capital expenditures, by far the best performing of the Magnificent Seven tech giants this year. Its shares are up 27 per cent in 2026, more than twice the gain of second place Nvidia, which is a key beneficiary of AI spending.

The outlays have gotten so large that companies like Alphabet and Amazon.com have seen their free cashflow turn negative, forcing them to increasingly turn to debt markets for funding. Meanwhile, rising interest rates are raising the cost of borrowing.

Apple, by contrast, is projected to see its free cash flow climb 38 per cent to $142 billion in fiscal 2026, which ended on Sep 30.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index fell 6.7 per cent in October, its worst month since March 2025.

CoreWeave and Nebius Group, data centre owners that offer AI computing services, have dropped more than 30 per cent this month. With Friday’s collapse, Intel lost more than 45 per cent in October, its biggest ever one-month drop in data compiled by Bloomberg going back more than 40 years. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Clar, Seatrium, Sheng Siong, MPACT, NetLink NBN, Starhill Global Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 30):

CapitaLand Ascendas Real Estate Investment Trust (Clar) : The trust on Thursday recorded higher rental reversion in the third quarter of 2026 amid its drive to reshape its industrial portfolio. Its rental reversion for Q3 came in at 9.9 per cent, up from 5.2 per cent in Q2, and 7.6 per cent the year before. For the first nine months of 2026, rental reversion was 9 per cent. Portfolio occupancy improved slightly, rising  to 90.1 per cent as at Sep 30, up from 89.1 per cent in the preceding quarter. But occupancy was still lower than the 91.3 per cent recorded the year before. Units of CapitaLand Ascendas Reit closed unchanged at S$2.18, before the business update.

Mi Material: The chip materials company posted on Thursday an adjusted profit after tax of US$11.4 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. This came on the back of US$37.8 million in revenue, representing a 15.6 per cent increase from before. The Singapore-headquartered company attributed the improved profitability to “sustained demand for its semiconductor packaging materials”. Its shares closed at S$1.80 on Thursday, down S$0.02 or 1.1 per cent.

Sheng Siong: The supermarket operator posted a Q3 profit of S$44.6 million, up 1.9 per cent from S$43.7 million the previous year. In a bourse filing on Thursday, the company reported S$441.5 million in revenue, up 6.2 per cent from S$415.5 million before. The group attributed the higher revenue to a rise in total stores in Singapore, as well as improvements in comparable same store sales. Within the city-state, it now has 92 stores, up from 84 stores previously. Sheng Siong shares closed Thursday at S$2.80, down S$0.04 or 1.4 per cent.

Seatrium : The offshore and marine engineering group said on Friday that it secured a contract worth more than S$200 million from SBM Offshore to carry out integration works on a floating production, storage and offloading vessel for offshore developments in South America. Work is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 and be completed in 2029. Shares of Seatrium closed S$0.01 or 0.6 per cent higher at S$1.84 on Thursday.

Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust (MPACT) : Its distribution per unit fell 3.5 per cent to S$0.0194 for the second quarter ended September, from S$0.0201 a year earlier. This was mainly due to weaker contributions from its overseas properties, particularly in Japan, China and Hong Kong, as well as the absence of income from assets divested in the previous financial year, said the manager. The decline was partially offset by stronger performance at VivoCity mall, following its basement two revamp, and lower financial expenses. Units of MPACT ended Thursday 0.9 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.13.

Netlink NBN Trust : The mainboard-listed trust reported on Thursday distribution per unit of S$0.0274 for its first half ended Sep 30, some 1.1 per cent higher than the corresponding period the year before. The increased distribution attributable to its unitholders came despite a 2.2 per cent drop in revenue, which came in at S$202.6 million for the half-year, compared with S$207.1 million in the year-ago period. The distribution will be paid to unitholders on Nov 24. The counter ended Thursday flat at S$0.93 before the announcement.

Starhill Global Reit : The manager reported a 2.3 per cent rise in the Reit’s net property income to S$38.8 million for the first quarter of 2027. In a Thursday bourse filing, the Reit manager also recorded a 1.2 per cent increase in revenue to S$48.9 million, from S$48.3 million in the previous corresponding period. The Reit’s improved performance was mainly driven by stronger contributions from its Singapore retail and Australia properties. Units of Starhill Global Reit closed unchanged at S$0.495 on Thursday.

Wilmar : The agribusiness group said on Thursday that it will voluntarily engage, at its own cost, an investigations firm and a law firm from the Government’s panel of assessors to examine whether it has any involvement in or connection with the Indonesian fires contributing to transboundary haze. Wilmar said it will give the assessors access to relevant documents, personnel and sites, and is ready to begin the inquiry once the National Environment Agency (NEA) issues its directions. Shares of Wilmar closed S$0.16 or 4.9 per cent lower at S$3.11 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil producer said on Thursday that its Singapore subsidiary received a notice from the National Environment Agency seeking information relating to the transboundary haze. Its Indonesian-listed subsidiary also received queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange over forest and land fires. The group said it had not identified any material impact from the fires and haze. Shares of Golden Agri-Resources closed S$0.005 or 1.8 per cent higher at S$0.28 on Thursday.

data.title: Issue 218: Potential winners in Singaporeâs grid investment plan; Singapore governance code review reveals proposals
data.description:
Energy transition

Energy sector’s brightening prospects

You know how there’s sometimes a superstar at work, and when this person leaves, it takes a few people to do the same job that one used to handle?

Fossil fuels are kind of like that superstar for energy, and headlines from Singapore International Energy Week suggest that it will take a multiple-alternatives strategy to transition away from the old standard.

Anticipation of an energy future marked by diversified technologies and rapidly growing demand could build a long-term bull case for energy-sector companies such as Sembcorp Industries, ST Engineering, Keppel Corp and EGP Energy.

Demand-led build-out

One of the most consequential announcements by Singapore is a comprehensive five-year Energy Infrastructure Plan that lays out a development strategy for the energy sector.

The impetus for the plan is that Singapore expects peak electricity demand to increase by 15 to 51 per cent over the next five years, with a forecast for peak demand to grow to between 9.9 and 13 gigawatts (GW) by 2031 from 8.6 GW as at Aug 2026. The main drivers of that increase are economic growth – underpinned by semiconductor industries and data centres – and the electrification of the transport sector.

In line with the rest of South-east Asia, Singapore faces a ballooning hunger for electricity, and this is driving massive investments that span not just different types of generation technologies, but also the different parts of the grid.

On the generation side, natural gas remains the main source of electricity. Singapore will open five new gas plants between 2026 and 2031 and is studying the feasibility of expanding its first liquefied natural gas terminal at Jurong Island.

In terms of low-carbon alternatives, Singapore has set a new 2035 target of 4 GW peak (GWp) for solar capacity by 2035, with its current 2.3 GWp capacity well on track towards the current target of 3 GWp by 2030. The country is also stepping up development of nuclear capabilities, and expanding research into geothermal solutions.

On transmission and distribution, Singapore’s new plan includes S$5.3 billion of expected investments between 2025 and 2029 to expand its power grid, which is 11 times the amount spent in the preceding five years. That money will go towards building seven new transmission substations by 2031, adding about 1,400 km to the transmission cable network and strengthening the distribution network. Furthermore, Singapore is looking into the feasibility of more than tripling the length of its cable tunnels from about 50 km today.

Multi-technology mix

The future energy landscape is likely to look significantly more heterogeneous, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that a portfolio approach is proving to be better from an energy security and resilience perspective. In Singapore’s case, disruptions from the Iran war and Indonesia’s throttling of gas exports are a clear reminder about the fragility of supply chains. Those vulnerabilities exist whether Singapore is importing green electricity, nuclear fuel or solar and battery equipment.

The second reason behind heterogeneity is that many of the options are imperfect. Nuclear is a relatively technologically mature and low-carbon source of energy, but it is also costly. Solar is relatively cheap, but Singapore’s solar capacity is much too little for the country’s needs. Hydrogen-based alternatives are costly as well, and some hydrogen carrier options such as ammonia come with significantly higher physical risks due to the dangers inherent in the fuel. Natural gas has a high carbon footprint, but it is available in the short term, a potential source of back-up power in the future and is the least carbon-intensive of the fossil fuels.

Any strategy to reduce reliance on fossil fuels may necessarily have to rely on a mix of options in order to be adequate, secure and resilient.

The same applies to energy storage systems. Researchers at the University of Utah suggest that a hybrid system that combines lithium ion batteries, pumped hydro storage and underground hydrogen storage may be more effective and cost efficient than single-technology solutions. The reason is that each storage technology is optimal under different conditions, and a hybrid approach allows the grid to better utilise the right tool at the right times.

Potential winners

The policy momentum suggests that the energy sector stands to receive significant investments in the years ahead, a substantial amount of which will be driven by the public sector. Public sector involvement could be as buyers, subsidy providers or as regulators and policymakers. Furthermore, the investments will flow to a broad swathe of the sector.

Those conditions could be especially favourable for companies that have broad capabilities across the infrastructure and energy space, as well as firms that have a track record of winning public-sector work.

Singapore-listed players Sembcorp, ST Engineering, Keppel and EGP Energy are some of the companies that could benefit.

Already, Sembcorp and ST Engineering have announced a knowledge exchange and potential partnership with Canada’s AtkinsRealis on tie-ups in the nuclear energy sector. Sembcorp, Keppel and Tuas Power Generation have also clinched a contract to import and supply biomethane as part of a 300-megawatt pilot to seek an alternative to natural gas under a sandbox framework.

Sembcorp’s utilities unit is also in a consortium with Malaysia’s national oil company Petronas and state utility Tenaga Nasional and with Vietnamese national oil company Petrovietnam Technical Services Corp that has just received conditional approval to import 1.3 GW of low-carbon electricity from Vietnam and Malaysia.

EGP Energy has been one of the best-performing initial public offerings on the Singapore market this year. On Oct 5, OCBC Group Research initiated coverage on the stock with a “buy” recommendation, citing the transmission and distribution equipment supplier’s strong presence in the Singapore extra high voltage and high voltage switchgear market.

Noting EGP Energy’s S$296.2 million order book at the time, OCBC analyst Heidi Mo said that the company’s 30-year relationship with Singapore’s national grid operator provides “capex visibility through 2030”.

Corporate governance

Singapore governance review aims at chairpersons, concurrent seats

A cap on concurrent directorships, stronger safeguards when board chairs are not independent and discouraged use of performance-linked share compensation for non-executive directors are among the recommendations by Singapore’s Corporate Governance Advisory Committee (CGAC) after a 17-month review.

Singapore Exchange (SGX) and CGAC are seeking public feedback on those recommendations. The public consultation ends Jan 27, 2027.

Key takeaways:

  • Cap concurrent directorships at five: CGAC recommends limiting the concurrent listed-company directorships held by any director to five. The consultation seeks feedback on whether the cap should be mandatory under the listing rules or comply-or-explain as a provision to the Code of Corporate Governance. The official estimate is that about 25 directors in 2024 held more than five board seats in listed companies. For context, in 2025 there were about 3,100 board directors on Singapore-listed companies.
  • Safeguards against non-independent chairs: A proposed listing rule change will make it compulsory for boards with non-independent chairs to appoint a lead independent director. An analysis by the Singapore Institute of Directors shows that in 2025, 70 listed entities, or just over 11 per cent of listed companies, had non-independent chairs but did not have lead independent directors.
  • Independent chairs on key board committees: The review recommends listing rule changes to mandate that the audit, nominating and remuneration board committees be led by independent directors and comprise a majority of independent directors. More than 95 per cent of these board committees already have independent chairs, and almost all have independent directors in the majority.
  • Capital management policy disclosure: The review recommends that companies maintain a capital management policy and to disclose it in the annual report, but is seeking feedback on whether this should be mandatory under the listing rules or comply-or-explain as a Code provision. If accepted as a listing rule, this will subsume a pending requirement effective January 2027 for companies to maintain and disclose a dividend policy.
  • No performance-based share compensation for non-executive directors: A proposed Code provision will state that non-executive directors should not receive performance-based share-based incentives and rewards. The aim is to avoid compromising the independence and objectivity of directors who are supposed to be overseeing performance outcomes. Non-performance-based share-based remuneration, such as share options that are not contingent on performance targets, would still be allowed. A study by the National University of Singapore’s Centre for Investor Protection of 510 listed entities shows about 16 per cent have non-independent, non-executive directors participating in share-based plans. Less than one per cent allow independent directors only to participate in share-based plans. About 62 companies allow independent directors to participate.
  • Enhanced risk disclosures: A proposed new Code provision will recommend that companies disclose a board assessment of principal and emerging risks and how those risks are managed.

On the whole, the elevation of a number of practices from comply-or-explain Code provisions to mandatory SGX listing rules represents a slight tightening of corporate governance practices. However, some have observed that the practices being elevated are mostly already widely adopted, which means that those elevated rules will not generate significant improvement from the current state of corporate governance.

The recommendations also include adding commentary about “intended outcomes” in response to feedback from focus groups that companies are not always clear about governance outcomes sought by the Code. For example, the Code on board membership will include an explanation that “a formal and transparent board appointment process, overseen by an objective and strongly independent nominating committee, ensures optimal board composition and progressive renewal”.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel, CICT, MLT, Golden-Agri, Wilmar, CDLHT, FEHT, UltraGreen.ai
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Oct 29):

Keppel : The asset manager and operator on Thursday reported a 20 per cent increase in its net profit for the third quarter ended Sep 30, 2026. Excluding its non-core portfolio for divestment and discontinued operations, net profit for “New Keppel” – the term the company uses to refer to its continuing core business – increased by close to 15 per cent year on year for the quarter. The increase in New Keppel’s profit was underpinned by stronger performance in its connectivity segment and steady earnings from its infrastructure segment, said the company. Shares of Keppel ended 0.3 per cent or S$0.03 higher at S$10.13 before the results.

CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (CICT) : Its net property income rose 13.8 per cent to S$334.9 million and revenue grew 15 per cent to S$464.5 million for the third quarter ended September. The manager attributed the increase to contributions from Paragon, which it acquired for S$3.9 billion in July this year; Gallileo, its commercial property in Germany, following asset enhancement works; and its increased stake in CapitaSpring. The counter ended Wednesday 0.4 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$2.26, before the business update.

Mapletree Logistics Trust (MLT) : The trust had a flat second quarter, with distribution per unit (DPU) of S$0.01816, up by 0.1 per cent, from S$0.01815 in the year-ago period. Distributable income grew 0.9 per cent to S$93.3 million for the quarter ended Sep 30, 2026, while revenue rose 1.4 per cent to S$180 million over the same period. Net property income rose one per cent to S$154.8 million. The increase was largely driven by contributions from the Mapletree Joo Koon Logistics Hub redevelopment, an acquisition in India, organic growth in Singapore, and currency appreciation of the renminbi and Australian dollar, said the manager. Units of MLT ended Wednesday 0.9 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.07, before the announcement.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil producer reaffirmed its commitment to cooperating fully and transparently with the Singapore authorities over matters related to the Indonesian forest fires and transboundary haze. It issued the statement after a meeting with Singapore government officials over transboundary haze. The group added that it shares the Singapore government’s concern about the impact of fires and transboundary haze and welcomes the opportunity to engage constructively with the relevant authorities and independent assessors. Shares of Golden Agri-Resources ended 1.9 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.275 before the announcement.

Wilmar : The agribusiness posted a net profit of US$281 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, reversing from a net loss of US$347.7 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Core net profit for the quarter fell 25.2 per cent to US$267.3 million from US$357.2 million, even as revenue grew 13.6 per cent to US$21.7 billion from US$19.1 billion. The group said its food products segment was hit by higher raw material costs, and the feed and industrial products segment, by weaker soybean crushing margins. Separately, the group said the fires in Indonesia and transboundary haze have neither resulted in, nor is expected to result in any material operational, financial, legal or regulatory impact on the company. Wilmar closed S$0.02 or 0.6 per cent higher at S$3.27, before the results.

CDL Hospitality Trusts (CDLHT): The trust posted a 7.1 per cent year-on-year increase in net property income to S$36.7 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$34.3 million a year earlier. Gross revenue rose 4.1 per cent to S$72 million, from S$69.2 million previously, the stapled group said in an operational update on Thursday. The improvement was driven by stronger contributions from its UK, New Zealand, Australian and European properties. Stapled securities of CDLHT closed flat at S$0.70 on Wednesday.

Far East Hospitality Trust (FEHT) : The trust on Thursday posted a 6.3 per cent rise in its Q3 net property income to S$27.6 million, from S$25.9 million the previous year. The group attributed this rise to higher gross revenue, which stood at S$32.6 million, up 7.2 per cent from S$30.4 million in the year-ago period. The increase in revenue was mainly driven by stronger performance at Four Points by Sheraton Nagoya, which was supported by demand from the Asian Games 2026. Units of FEHT closed 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Wednesday.

UltraGreen.ai : Medtech platform UltraGreen.ai reported a 43.9 per cent growth in Q3 2026 revenue to US$44.6 million from US$31 million in Q3 2025 in a bourse filing on Thursday. This growth consisted of a 47 per cent increase from the US market from US$23.9 million in Q3 2025 to US$35.2 million in Q3 2026. The rest of world revenue contribution grew 32 per cent from US$7.1 million in Q3 2025 to US$9.4 million in Q3 2026. Shares of UltraGreen.ai closed up 7.6 per cent or US$0.04 at US$0.565 on Wednesday.
